options.misconception: Assuming includes uses strict reference only for objects

questions.explanation: includes reports whether a value is present using same-value matching, so finding 2994 yields true. indexOf would return the position instead of a boolean. The printed value is true, while the alternatives come from assuming includes uses strict reference only for objects, returning the found element and returning an index-style position.
questions.hint: includes returns a boolean, not a position.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — slice.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 2996.

options.misconception: Treating the slice end index as included
Assuming slice returns a copy of everything
Treating the start index as the end

questions.explanation: slice takes elements from index 1 up to but not including index 3, which is two elements. The end boundary is exclusive, a common source of off-by-one confusion. The printed value is 2, while the alternatives come from treating the slice end index as included, treating the start index as the end and assuming slice returns a copy of everything.
questions.hint: The second argument of slice is not part of the result.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — splice.

options.misconception: Reporting the count of removed items instead
Assuming splice leaves the array unchanged
Removing one item instead of two

questions.explanation: splice removes two elements starting at index 1 and returns them, leaving 3 elements. Unlike slice, splice changes the original array in place. The printed value is 3, while the alternatives come from assuming splice leaves the array unchanged, reporting the count of removed items instead and removing one item instead of two.
questions.hint: splice is destructive: the original array shrinks by the removed count.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — map.

options.misconception: Assuming map returns the original element

questions.explanation: map applies the doubling callback to every element and returns a new array, so the first output is 2998 times two, or 5996. The source array is not changed. The printed value is 5996, while the alternatives come from assuming map returns the original element, adding instead of multiplying and dividing rather than doubling.
questions.hint: map builds a new array from each callback result.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving arrays — filter.
questions.explanation: filter keeps only values strictly greater than 99; exactly 2 of the three entries qualify. Elements equal to the threshold are rejected by the strict comparison. Carrying the operation through gives 2; common slips include assuming every element passes the test and counting rejected items instead of kept ones.
questions.hint: Check each element against the strict greater-than test.
